title: Late payment bill would cap business terms at 60 days and make base rate plus 8% interest compulsory, but the cheque is not in the post yet
seo_title: Late payment bill: 60-day cap and compulsory 8% interest
dek: The government says the Commercial Payments Bill, branded the Small Business Protections Bill, would cap business payment terms at 60 days and make 8% over base rate interest mandatory on late payments. It was still in the Lords in August, the latest we could check, and the cap is planned for 2027 at the earliest.
summary: The late payment bill would cap business payment terms at 60 days and make 8% over base interest mandatory. In the Lords in August; cap not before 2027.
body:
The government says its late payment bill would cap payment terms between businesses at 60 days, with limited exemptions, and make interest on late payments mandatory at 8% above the Bank of England base rate. It would also give the Small Business Commissioner new powers to investigate and adjudicate disputes, and to fine persistent late payers. The latest stage we could confirm is the House of Lords in August, and on the government's own plan the cap would not start before 2027.

Its formal name is the Commercial Payments Bill. The [Department for Business and Trade's press release](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/largest-crackdown-on-late-payments-in-over-25-years-as-landmark-bill-enters-parliament) of 19 May 2026 branded it the Small Business Protections Bill, which is the name you are more likely to have heard, and said it was due to be introduced in the House of Lords on Tuesday 19 May. A [BCLP briefing](https://www.bclplaw.com/en-US/events-insights-news/commercial-payments-bill-and-its-impact-on-construction-contracts.html) written in mid-August says it was, that it had its second reading on 9 June, and that it completed its Committee stage on 21 July 2026, when a new version was published. When BCLP wrote, no date had been announced for Report stage.

Where it stands today we cannot say for certain. Parliament's bill pages and Hansard would not open for us before publishing, so anything after mid-August is not in our facts. Nothing we have read suggests it has become law, but we could not check that for today either.

## What the bill would change

We have not been able to read the bill itself. What follows is the government's account, and BCLP's reading of the 21 July version.

**The cap.** The press release pitches it as a 60-day cap "on all large firms paying smaller suppliers". The government's [consultation response](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/late-payments-tackling-poor-payment-practices/outcome/late-payment-consultation-time-to-pay-up-government-response-web-version), updated 24 July 2026, puts it more broadly: it intends "a maximum payment term of 60 days between businesses, with limited exemptions". The exemptions it intends are where both parties are large companies, where the purchaser is the smaller party, and where the goods or services are imported or exported.

A tighter 45-day limit is parked rather than dropped: "We do not intend to take this forward now but may revisit it in the future." On timing, the response describes "a gradual change with an appropriate transition period, starting with 60 days, no earlier than 2027." That is the government's plan for a phase-in, not a commencement date in law.

**Public bodies.** Sixty days is not the only number. BCLP reads the 21 July version as setting a maximum of 30 days for public authorities, where the contract is not covered by the Procurement Act 2023, and 60 days for everyone else, subject to the limited exemptions. Neither government page we read mentions the 30-day figure, so treat it as BCLP's reading of a text we have not checked ourselves.

**Interest.** Statutory interest is not new. Under [section 1 of the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/20/section/1), it is an implied term of a contract the Act applies to that "any qualifying debt created by the contract carries simple interest". The catch is [section 8](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/20/section/8): a term that excludes the right is void "unless there is a substantial contractual remedy for late payment of the debt". So today a contract can swap statutory interest for a remedy of its own, as long as that remedy is substantial.

What changes is that the government intends to "remove the ability for parties to agree an alternative remedy to statutory interest", so the right could no longer be written out of a contract. BCLP reads the bill the same way, with paying parties subject to the "full statutory rate (8% above the Bank of England base rate)".

That 8% is the government's figure and BCLP's. The Act itself names no number: [section 6](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/20/section/6) leaves the rate to be set "by order made with the consent of the Treasury", and we have not traced that order, so we have not checked the 8% against it.

**The commissioner.** The press release talks of "potential fines that could be worth tens of millions for persistently late payers". That is a potential figure, not a cap, and nothing we read gives a statutory maximum. BCLP's list of the powers adds adjudication "outside of the court process" and "binding interim decisions".

**Retentions.** The press release lists a ban on withholding retention payments under construction contracts. The consultation response is more careful: "we propose to ban" the practice, and the government is consulting on its implementation. BCLP reads the 21 July text as phasing it in: retention clauses can still be agreed during years one and two, and "they will automatically become ineffective at the end of year three". Whether your set build counts as a construction contract is a question for whoever writes your contracts.

The government's own estimate of what late payment costs the UK economy is almost £11 billion a year.

## What we make of it

The interest change is the one that matters most to freelancers, and it is not the one in the headlines. Plenty of crew know they can charge statutory interest and never do, because billing a regular client for it feels like resigning by invoice. The bill will not cure that. What it would do is stop the right being written out of the contract before you have even seen the job sheet.

We would take a commissioner who can fine over another code of practice. Whether it changes behaviour depends on the fines actually landing, and on whether anyone at the bottom of a chain is willing to complain about the client at the top of it.

Sixty days is still two months, which is a long wait for a day rate earned in a loading bay at 5am. It beats the 90-day terms some of us have learnt to live with from big agencies.

The exemptions are where the detail will bite. This is our reading of the intended wording, not of the bill: the both-parties-large exemption leaves the middle of a supply chain exposed, so a large AV supplier could be capped when it pays crew but not when its large client pays it. The export exemption may matter for touring and cross-border kit hire. We would not plan around either until the bill's definitions are pinned down, and we have not been able to check its text for this piece.

What happens next is forecasting, and BCLP's dates from August. It thinks amendment is more likely in the Commons. It also thought it unlikely the bill would reach the Commons before early 2027, and expected it to become law "if all goes to plan, at some point during 2027".

Until it is law, the invoice is still yours to chase.

confirmed.text: The government's press release of 19 May 2026 says the Small Business Protections Bill is formally the Commercial Payments Bill and was due to be introduced in the House of Lords on Tuesday 19 May.
The press release lists a 60-day cap on payment terms for all large firms paying smaller suppliers, and mandatory interest on late payments set at 8% above the Bank of England base rate.

The press release promises the Small Business Commissioner powers to investigate, adjudicate disputes and fine persistent late payers, with potential fines that could be worth tens of millions; it gives no statutory maximum.

The government's consultation response (updated 24 July 2026) intends a maximum payment term of 60 days between businesses, with exemptions where both parties are large companies, where the purchaser is the smaller party, or where the goods or services are imported or exported.

The consultation response describes a gradual change with a transition period, starting with 60 days, no earlier than 2027, and says a reduction to 45 days is not being taken forward now but may be revisited in the future.

The consultation response intends to remove the ability for parties to agree an alternative remedy to statutory interest, and frames the retention ban as a proposal, with the government consulting on its implementation.
The consultation response estimates that late payments cost the UK economy almost £11 billion a year.

BCLP reports that the bill was introduced in the House of Lords on 19 May 2026, had its second reading on 9 June and completed its Committee stage on 21 July, when a new version was published; in mid-August no Report stage date had been announced.

BCLP reads the bill as setting a maximum of 30 days for public authorities where the contract is not covered by the Procurement Act 2023, and 60 days for non-public authorities, subject to limited exemptions.

Section 1(1) of the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 makes it an implied term of a contract the Act applies to that any qualifying debt created by the contract carries simple interest.
Section 6(1) of the 1998 Act does not state the 8% figure; it has the rate set by order made with the consent of the Treasury.
Section 8(1) of the 1998 Act makes contract terms that exclude the right to statutory interest void unless there is a substantial contractual remedy for late payment of the debt.

speculation.text: BCLP's authors think amendment of the bill is more likely in the House of Commons.
BCLP's authors, writing in August 2026, thought it unlikely the bill would move to the House of Commons before early 2027.
BCLP's authors expect the bill to become law, if all goes to plan, at some point during 2027.

impact:
**Freelance crew.** As we read it (no source we read says so in terms), nothing changes on today's invoices: the terms you have agreed stand until the bill is law and in force, and the government plans to start the cap no earlier than 2027. Our advice in the meantime, which is ours and not the bill's: put your payment terms on every quote and invoice instead of leaving them to the client's purchase order, and add a line reserving your right to statutory interest under the 1998 Act, which you have now. Read the client's terms too, because under section 8 a contract can still replace that right with a substantial remedy of its own. Keep a simple log of who paid late and by how long. If the commissioner gets its new powers, a record with dates in it will be worth more than a grievance in the group chat.

**Crew chiefs and small suppliers who book other freelancers.** The press release talks about large firms paying smaller suppliers; the consultation response talks about businesses in general, with an exemption where the buyer is the smaller party. If the bill follows the response, you could be inside the cap when you pay your own crew. The bill text decides, and we have not checked it.

**Production companies and AV suppliers.** Watch the middle of the chain. On our reading of the intended exemption, if you and your client both count as large, the client's terms to you may not be capped, while your terms to smaller crew and suppliers could be. Look at cash flow before 2027 rather than during it.

**Corporate event teams.** If your organisation counts as large, standard terms longer than 60 days for small suppliers look to us to be on borrowed time, so procurement may as well start the conversation now. On BCLP's reading, public authorities face a 30-day maximum where the contract is not covered by the Procurement Act 2023, so a council or other public-sector event client may be on the shorter limit.

**Touring and overseas work.** The intended import and export exemption could take cross-border jobs outside the cap. That depends on definitions we have not seen, so do not count on it either way.

**The build side.** If your contracts carry retentions and count as construction contracts, BCLP reads the bill as banning retentions after a transition, with retention clauses still possible in years one and two. The government says it is still consulting on how the ban would be implemented.

Before relying on any detail here, read the bill as it now stands on parliament.uk.
verdict_note: Still in the Lords in August, the latest we could check, and on the government's plan the cap starts no earlier than 2027. Meanwhile, put your terms and a statutory interest line on every invoice: the 1998 Act gives you that right today, unless a contract swaps it for a substantial remedy.
